strengths: Significant and timely resource contribution: Common Corpus (~2T tokens, 517M documents) is the largest openly licensed, multilingual pre-training corpus, addressing a real and increasingly urgent problem (copyright/ToS restrictions, dataset takedowns) that motivates much of the paper.

Unusually thorough provenance and legal documentation: per-dataset sources (Appendices A-C), per-document license metadata, an explicit public-domain verification process (author life+70, pre-1884 rule, US 95-year rule, no digitization rights), and adherence to emerging dataset best practices (Baack et al., 2025). This level of rights diligence is rare and sets a standard for the field.

Real demonstrated impact: the corpus has already been used to train multiple European LLMs/SLMs (e.g., Salamandra, Lucie), fine-tuned models (NeKo), and downstream datasets (FineVideo, MOSEL), and was adopted by industry (Anthropic), which substantiates the 'critical infrastructure' claim better than hypothetical use cases.

Releases a set of useful accompanying tools and models (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon) for OCR quality estimation, correction, PII removal, and toxicity filtering, which are independently valuable for the community.

Multilingual emphasis (including low-resource European languages) with no machine translation, plus historical/temporal metadata enabling dated language models, differentiates it from monolingual permissive efforts (OLC, KL3M, Common Pile).
weaknesses: Anonymization/copy-editing quality problems: several author names and model names appear to have been stripped incompletely (e.g., 'As [blank] was one of the contributors...', 'Two models derived from [blank], and [blank]'), leaving the text broken; there are also typos and inconsistencies ('Sentence Neuron' for SentencePiece, 'Loukas' vs. Loukas, duplicated Longpre 2024b/c references, 'coposed', 'OCPoscope', 'OCRerrcr' vs. 'OCReRRcr'). This is sloppy for a camera-ready-quality submission.

Limited direct empirical evaluation: the paper is essentially a technical report; there are no controlled experiments (e.g., ablations on the curation pipeline, perplexity or downstream benchmarks of models trained on Common Corpus vs. comparable permissive corpora like Common Pile or OLC). Claims about quality are largely delegated to cited third-party projects.

Curation quality is asserted rather than rigorously measured: e.g., OCRoscope reports only 59% non-recognized 7-grams (vs. 85% self-estimated by BnF), and OCR correction (OCRonos) or synthetic rewriting of historical texts risks hallucination/content drift, but there is no quantitative fidelity evaluation on held-out data.

Data quality risks are acknowledged but not quantified: the heavy reliance on OCR'd 18th-19th century newspapers (~460B+ tokens of Open Culture) implies substantial noise; the composition table shows token counts but not deduplication statistics, contamination checks, or per-source quality scores.

Web license re-identification (the acknowledged weakness of C4C/CCCC-style efforts) is deferred to future work, so the Open Web collection is small and the paper's strongest claims rest on public-domain/government/code sources.

Some framing overreach: 'ethical' in the title is contentious (licensing compliance is not the same as ethical data), and the 'open data paradox' argument, while interesting, is informal; ethical concerns regarding historical toxic content are handled via a classifier (Celadon) whose effect on the corpus is not reported with filtering statistics.

strengths: Genuinely valuable resource: ~2 trillion tokens of uncopyrighted/permissively licensed data across six collections, with per-document license and provenance metadata, which fills a real gap as legal takedowns (Books3, MATH, GEITje) erode the AI data commons.
Multilingual coverage (French, German, Spanish, plus low-resource and historical languages) distinguishes it from monolingual open efforts like Open License Corpus, KL3M, or Common Pile.

Thorough provenance documentation: appendices detail source-by-source token counts, languages, and time ranges, and Appendix C lays out an explicit, auditable rights-verification methodology (author life + 70 years, pre-1884 rule, US publication + 95 years, no digitization rights).

Useful auxiliary tooling released alongside the dataset (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon, PII replacement pipeline), addressing issues (OCR quality, PII, toxicity in historical text) that most pre-training corpora ignore.
Demonstrated real-world adoption (Salamandra, Lucie, Anthropic feature visualization, speech datasets), lending credibility to the 'critical infrastructure' claim.
weaknesses: Very weak empirical evaluation for a top-tier venue: no head-to-head comparison of models trained on Common Corpus vs. comparable web corpora (C4, RefinedWeb, Dolma) at matched scale; impact claims rest on anecdotes and external projects whose results are not independently analyzed. The t-SNE plot (Fig. 2b) is decorative rather than evaluative.

Data quality claims are unsupported by quantitative audits. No deduplication analysis or duplicate rate statistics are reported at all for a 2T-token corpus—an omission that is hard to excuse given how much of the content comes from overlapping newspaper/book digitizations. The OCR quality assessment (59% rate vs. the BnF's self-estimated 85%) is presented with almost no methodological detail, and OCRonos correction is illustrated only with cherry-picked examples, with no measured correction accuracy or hallucination rate on held-out data.

The PII pipeline is evaluated with a single unexplained number ('increased this accuracy to 85%') with no definition of accuracy, no test set, and no error analysis—despite the paper claiming GDPR compliance as a core contribution.

Inconsistencies and gaps in token accounting: footnote 2 (how token counts were computed) is cut off/unnamed; Table 3 mixes overlapping license categories (CC-By vs. CC-BY-4.0; 'Open license' undefined); the '2 trillion tokens' headline number cannot be fully verified from the paper.

Several central claims rely on unnamed/redacted artifacts (e.g., 'the models in the [name] family', 'Two models derived from [name] and [name] are currently leading evaluations'), which makes the Impact section unverifiable and self-serving; the 'currently leading evaluations in their size range' claim cites no benchmark, no numbers, and no comparison methodology.

License verification is asserted rather than demonstrated: no error rate, sampling audit, or disagreement analysis for the automated/public-domain determination process is provided, even though the entire legal-compliance value proposition rests on it. The acknowledged risk that CC license mentions on web pages may not cover entire pages (Section 3.5) is left unquantified.

Significant content-quality risk is acknowledged but not measured: a large share of tokens comes from 18th–19th century OCR'd newspapers whose usable-data rate the authors' own citations suggest may be below 50%; the paper never reports what fraction of the 2T tokens survives its own quality pipelines.

Writing and positioning issues: the introduction contains a citation error ('Sentence Neuron (Radford et al., 2017)' following 'GPT-1 (Radford et al.)' with no year), inconsistent license naming, typos ('coposed', 'reguations', 'fictuous', 'OCPoscope'), and heavy reliance on the authors' own prior work (Arnett et al., Gallicagram, French-PD) for methods that are only summarized here.
The 'largest' claim depends on the authors' own counting and scope choices and is not rigorously benchmarked against KL3M (1.2T) or Common Pile (1T) in terms of comparable, verified tokens.

strengths: Significant and timely contribution: Common Corpus is, to the authors' (well-supported) claim, the largest openly licensed pre-training corpus (~2T tokens), and the only one at this scale that is multilingual, addressing a genuine and growing need given legal pressure on the AI data commons (e.g., Consent in Crisis results cited in the paper).

Exceptional provenance documentation: the paper (and appendices) meticulously documents sources, token counts, languages, license types, and per-source curation decisions, going well beyond the documentation standards of prior corpora such as The Pile, C4, or Dolma.

Careful legal/rights treatment: the internal rights verification process for public-domain cultural heritage data (Appendix C), including author-life+70 rules, the 1884 cutoff, and the 'no digitization rights' principle grounded in the 2019 EU Copyright Directive, is a substantive methodological contribution for licensed data collection.

Realistic curation tooling with practical value: the released tools (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon) address a real gap — OCR-quality issues in digitized cultural data — and the OCRonos correction examples in Appendix D are convincing demonstrations.

Demonstrated impact: the corpus has already been used by multiple independent projects (Salamandra, Lucie, NeKo, Mosel/FAMA, Anthropic), providing external validation of the resource's utility, which is stronger evidence than internal benchmarks alone.
Honest limitations section: the 'open data paradox' framing, acknowledgment of shallow low-resource language coverage, and caveats about curation accuracy are appropriately transparent.
weaknesses: No experimental evaluation in the paper itself: there are no benchmark results, no data-quality audits (e.g., no replication of the Kreutzer et al. style quality audit on the authors' own multilingual data), and no ablations of the cleaning pipeline. Claims about downstream usefulness rest on citations to other projects' reports rather than controlled experiments.

Significant presentation defects that suggest a rushed submission: several sentences are missing words or entire entities (e.g., 'As [blank] was one of the contributors at the Dataset Convening', 'models in the [blank] family', 'Two models derived from [blank] and [blank]', Celadon 'released as parts of a separate work .' with a dangling empty citation, incomplete footnote 2 about tokenizer/token counts). These redactions appear intentional but substantially harm readability and reproducibility of claims.

Internal inconsistencies and errors: the reported OCR quality of ~59% non-recognized 7-grams on processed content is alarming given the corpus's stated purpose, and the discrepancy with the French National Library's self-estimated 85% is not reconciled; typos ('coposed', 'reguations', 'Open Govenment', 'trillon', 'OCPoscope', 'fictuous', 'theses projects') recur throughout.

Title overclaims: 'Ethical Data' in the title is normative and not fully supported — the paper documents licensing rigor but the corpus still contains historical texts with harmful content (acknowledged in Section 4.5) and OCR noise; a more neutral framing ('permissively licensed') would be more defensible.

Some license categories are ambiguous or potentially problematic: 'Open license' as a bucket (10.4B tokens) is undefined; mixing CC-By variants into a single 'CC-By' row while also listing 'CC-BY-4.0' separately is inconsistent; the treatment of CC-By-SA and share-alike obligations for downstream model training is not discussed.

Reproducibility gaps for the curation pipeline: filters are described qualitatively but thresholds, precision/recall of OCRerrcr and Celadon are not reported in this paper (deferred to other works), making it hard to assess how much data is lost or corrupted by each stage.

Scoping imbalance: the corpus is heavily skewed toward European languages and public-domain historical text (mostly pre-1900 cultural data and government/legal documents); the paper acknowledges this but the practical domain shift relative to web-crawl-based corpora is not analyzed.

strengths: Significant and timely contribution: Common Corpus is, to the authors' demonstrated knowledge, the largest (~2T token) fully permissively-licensed, multilingual, multi-domain pre-training corpus, filling a genuine gap identified by prior work (e.g., Longpre et al. 2024's 'Consent in Crisis'), and uniquely combining open licensing with multilingual and beyond-web-crawl coverage (Table 1).

Exceptional provenance documentation: every collection (Open Government, Culture, Science, Code, Web, Semantic) is detailed with sources, licenses, languages, token counts, and footnoted links; the Open Culture rights-verification criteria (Appendix E) provide a concrete, reproducible methodology for public-domain determination that the community can reuse.

Release of substantial supporting artifacts and tools: the Bad Data Toolbox (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon) addresses real problems specific to digitized/historical/multilingual data, going beyond simple aggregation and giving reusable value beyond this dataset.

Evidence of non-triviality: trained 350M and 1.2B Llama-style models (~1T tokens) on the corpus; competitive or superior MultiBLiMP results vs. comparably-sized and even larger models (e.g., outperforming OLMo 1B), with per-language results in appendices supporting the multilingual quality claim.

Honest limitations section and responsible practices: PII removal with documented recall improvements, toxicity filtering tailored to historical public-domain text, tokenizer fertility analysis, and explicit acknowledgment that the corpus is not sufficient for larger models.
weaknesses: The headline evaluation does not validate the headline resource: the trained models use a 'filtered subset' of ~1T tokens (plus multiple epochs for the 1.2B), so the paper never demonstrates that the full ~2T corpus, or its most distinctive components (historical OCR text, Open Semantic), is beneficial; no ablation comparing Common Corpus vs. FineWeb-2/Dolma-style data at matched scale, which is the controlled experiment a datasets paper ideally provides.

Benchmark coverage is narrow (MultiBLiMP, XStoryCloze, XCOPA); on XStoryCloze and XCOPA 'Ours' models clearly trail Gemma 3 at every scale, and the claim of 'comparable performance' leans heavily on one benchmark; no perplexity, domain/language-stratified perplexity, or downstream knowledge tasks (e.g., multilingual MMLU-style), and no evaluation of code-capable behavior despite ~283B code tokens.

Comparison fairness concerns: baseline models differ in tokenizer, vocabulary (65k vs. 256k for Gemma 3), training token count, architecture, and data epoch count, making cross-model conclusions about data quality weakly supported; reported training compute (2944 vs. 23040 H100 hours) suggests non-matched regimes.

Some central claims are asserted rather than evidenced: 'negligible rate of duplication' is attributed to curation without a systematic dedup study or fuzzy-duplicate measurements; the PII replacement with 'fictitious but realistic values' is not evaluated for residual leakage or distortion; legal compliance is claimed ('in compliance with even the strictest AI regulations') without legal expert validation, which is a strong claim for a paper of this nature.

Practicality/usability questions under-addressed: most content is pre-1884 historical OCR text whose model-quality impact is unquantified (OCRonos corrections are LLM-generated rewrites that could contaminate the corpus); no discussion of storage/distribution scale, versioning policy, or maintenance plan; references to repositories are rendered as placeholder emoji icons in the manuscript, which undermines verifiability of released artifacts.

Novelty beyond aggregation is moderate: several tools and subsets were released in prior separate works (Celadon/ToxicCommons, German PD Newspapers, Europeana Newspapers), and much of the corpus re-uses existing resources (The Stack, OpenAlex, S2ORC-adjacent sets), so the incremental technical contribution is primarily in curation methodology and rights verification.

strengths: The corpus is a substantial and unique resource: ~2 trillion tokens of uncopyrighted or permissively licensed data, multilingual (top-50 languages documented with per-language counts), and multi-domain, filling a genuine gap given the decline of the AI data commons documented in the cited literature.

Thorough provenance documentation: each collection (Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Code, Open Web, Open Semantic) is described with sources, licenses, languages, and token counts (Tables 3-10), and internal rights-verification criteria for public-domain cultural data are explicitly stated (Appendix E).

The paper goes beyond a dataset dump by releasing curation tooling (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon) with detailed descriptions and examples, addressing problems (OCR noise, toxicity, PII) that are usually neglected in open-licensed corpora.

Models trained on the corpus show strong multilingual grammatical competence on MultiBLiMP relative to size, with extensive per-language results (Tables 11-12), supporting the claim that the corpus is usable for multilingual pretraining.
The discussion of legal risk, takedowns (Books3, MATH, LAION, GEITje), and the 'open data paradox' provides useful context and motivation for the open-data research community.
weaknesses: The empirical validation of the dataset is thin. Only three benchmarks (MultiBLiMP, XStoryCloze, XCOPA) are used, and the models actually underperform Gemma 3 on XStoryCloze and XCOPA at matched or smaller scale (e.g., 350M vs. 270M; 1.2B vs. 1B). The framing of 'comparable performance' and 'outstanding performance on MultiBLiMP' overstates what the tables show; no knowledge-intensive or downstream tasks (e.g., multilingual QA, MMLU-style suites) are evaluated, where dataset diversity claims would be more directly tested.

No ablations or controlled experiments isolate the contribution of the curation pipeline: there is no comparison of model quality with/without OCR correction, toxicity filtering, PII replacement with fictitious values (which plausibly harms model understanding of real PII, and the claimed mitigation is untested), or the ~1T-token 'filtered subset' vs. the full 2T corpus. The training recipe details (learning rate, mixture, filtering thresholds) are largely absent.

Key quality claims are asserted rather than evidenced: 'negligible rate of duplication' based on 'early experiments' with no numbers or methodology; 'Most data objects present high peaks at similar proportions in the expected range' (Figure 4) is a qualitative statement with no baseline comparison against other corpora; the t-SNE plot (Figure 3b) and domain-overlap analysis (<2% of FineWeb domains) are anecdotal.

The comparison in Table 1 is somewhat self-serving: 'Open data' as the sole distinguishing axis against FineWeb 2/DCAD-2000 conflates licensing with quality, and the paper does not quantify how much of the corpus (beyond the license table) would survive stricter scrutiny of the public-domain determination heuristics (e.g., the flat 'all publications after 1884' rule, US-only author attribution via Wikidata).

Manuscript quality issues undermine credibility: numerous broken/placeholder references and footnotes (URLs replaced with emoji placeholders, missing tokenizer and repository links), inconsistencies ('OCRerrcr' vs 'OCRRerrcr' vs 'OCRerrcr', 'Open Govenment', 'difersity'), and an incomplete evaluation section referencing per-language appendix tables that are the main quantitative evidence.

The benchmark selection weakly favors the model family: MultiBLiMP rewards grammatical-minimal-pair performance, where curated, low-noise, historically rich text plausibly helps, but this advantage does not transfer to the general reasoning benchmarks, which is not honestly acknowledged in the main text.

Significance for the top-tier venue is arguable: the corpus itself may be impactful as infrastructure, but as a scientific contribution the paper is primarily a technical report; the training experiments (2 models, single seeds, no scaling analysis) are insufficient to support claims about data quality or scaling behavior.

strengths: Massive and unique resource: Common Corpus is ~2T tokens of permissively licensed/public-domain multilingual data, clearly the largest fully open pre-training corpus, with strong multilingual coverage (50+ languages with meaningful token counts, several low-resource and historical languages).

Exceptional provenance and documentation: the paper details sources, license verification procedures (including explicit public-domain criteria such as author life + 70 years and the 1884 cutoff), and per-subset token/language statistics in extensive appendices — a model for responsible dataset documentation.

Real contribution of novel content: the corpus deliberately sources PDF-heavy, curated collections (government, cultural heritage, science, Wikidata in natural language) with <2% page overlap with FineWeb domains, addressing the 'open data paradox' rather than re-filtering Common Crawl.

Substantial engineering contributions released as tools (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon), including OCR quality detection/correction pipelines that address a genuine problem for digitized public-domain data and should be useful beyond this corpus.

Validation by pre-training two models (350M, 1.2B) and evaluation on multilingual benchmarks (MultiBLiMP, XStoryCloze, XCOPA), with competitive results against comparably sized models (XGLM, BLOOM, OLMo), supporting the claim that the data is suitable for multilingual pre-training.

Strong positioning: clear motivation from legal/regulatory pressures (DMCA takedowns, ToS restrictions, consent decline) and a careful comparison table against KL3M, Dolma, C4, ROOTS, DCAD-2000, FineWeb 2, and Common Pile, showing Common Corpus is the only dataset satisfying all four openness criteria.
Reproducibility is good in spirit: tokenizers, models, curation tools, and dataset artifacts are stated to be publicly released, and per-language benchmark results are fully reported.
weaknesses: Evaluation is relatively thin for a top-tier venue: only three benchmarks (MultiBLiMP, XStoryCloze, XCOPA), all fairly narrow linguistic/completion tasks. No multilingual knowledge or reasoning benchmarks (e.g., multilingual MMLU-style tasks, FLORES perplexity, world-knowledge probes), so claims about general pre-training utility rest on limited evidence.

Baseline comparisons are confounded: Gemma 3, XGLM, and BLOOM were trained on vastly different data and compute; the 1.2B model is trained on 'Common Corpus and three epochs of the filtered subset', blurring attribution of performance to Common Corpus itself. A controlled comparison against training the same architecture on e.g. FineWeb-2 or OLMo's data at matched compute would substantially strengthen the claim.

The 350M/1.2B models are trained on ~1T tokens (a filtered subset), not the full 2T corpus, so the released models do not validate the complete dataset; the effect of the filtering applied before model training is not ablated.

Some curation choices are described but not quantitatively validated: OCRonos' correction quality is shown only via examples (with acknowledged risk of becoming a 'rewriting tool'), Celadon's toxicity filtering is validated in separate work, and deduplication claims ('negligible rate') lack supporting numbers.

PII replacement with 'fictitious but realistic values' and LLM-based OCR correction introduce potential synthetic-content contamination into a corpus marketed as verifiable/auditable; the paper would benefit from discussion of the provenance implications of LLM-rewritten text for downstream auditability.
Language identification relies on fastText/cld2, which is known to be noisy for low-resource languages and historical text; per-language accuracy of the language tags is not evaluated.

Minor issues: several dataset/URL references appear incomplete or redacted in the manuscript; comparison models in Table 1 are characterized somewhat coarsely; the 'open data paradox' argument is more observational than analyzed quantitatively.
Significance is primarily as infrastructure/resource rather than as a scientific result; impact depends on community uptake, though the preliminary model results mitigate this concern.
